blocks.text: You may be asked to:
Counsel a woman who had unprotected sexual intercourse 24–48 hours ago.
Advise a patient whose condom broke during intercourse.
Discuss emergency contraception with a woman who missed several contraceptive pills.
Choose an appropriate emergency contraceptive for a patient presenting 4 days after intercourse.
Counsel a woman who is breastfeeding or taking enzyme-inducing medication.
Explain emergency contraception following sexual assault.
Counsel a woman who vomited after taking emergency contraception.
Your main objective: identify the timing and circumstances of pregnancy risk, offer the most appropriate method, explain its effectiveness and limitations, and arrange appropriate follow-up.
Begin by establishing rapport and ensuring privacy.
Example opening:

“Hello, my name is Dr ____. I understand you would like advice about emergency contraception. I can explain the available options, how they work, their effectiveness and any possible side effects. I will also ask a few questions to help us choose the most appropriate option for you. Is that okay?”
Demonstrate empathy and avoid judgement. Do not assume the patient is married, sexually active by choice, or using contraception incorrectly.
If sexual assault is disclosed, prioritise immediate safety, supportive care, consent and access to appropriate sexual-assault services.
Use the following structure to ensure you do not miss important information.
When did the unprotected intercourse occur?
Was it a single episode or were there multiple episodes?
Was a condom used, and did it break or slip?
Was ejaculation intravaginal?
Was there any other unprotected intercourse earlier in the current menstrual cycle?
Why this matters: emergency contraceptive options depend on the time since intercourse, while earlier episodes may alter the assessment of possible existing pregnancy.
Ask about:
First day of the last menstrual period.
Usual cycle length and regularity.
Whether the period is overdue.
Symptoms suggesting pregnancy.
Recent pregnancy, miscarriage, abortion or delivery, where relevant.
Do not rely solely on menstrual dates to exclude pregnancy.
Ask whether the patient uses:
Combined oral contraceptive pills.
Progestogen-only pills.
Injectable contraception.
An implant.
An intrauterine contraceptive device.
Condoms or another method.
Clarify missed pills, delayed injections, a displaced or expelled device, or any other contraceptive failure.

content_groups.group_title: D. Relevant medical history and medicines

blocks.text: Ask about:
Current medicines, particularly enzyme-inducing drugs.
Recent use of hormonal contraception.
Breastfeeding.
Allergies and relevant medical conditions.
Previous ectopic pregnancy or other relevant gynaecological history.
Examples of enzyme-inducing medicines include rifampicin or rifabutin, certain anti-seizure medicines and St John's wort. These can reduce the effectiveness of oral emergency contraception.
Ask sensitively about:
Possible sexually transmitted infection (STI) exposure.
Whether the intercourse was consensual.
Whether the patient feels safe.
Whether she would like STI testing or additional support.
OSCE tip: obtain only the information needed for safe care, explain confidentiality and its limits, and avoid interrogating or blaming the patient.
There are three main options to discuss.
The most effective established method of emergency contraception.
Usually inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse, or within 5 days of estimated ovulation under applicable guidance.
Provides ongoing contraception after insertion.
Requires assessment and insertion by a trained clinician.
Consider STI risk, pregnancy exclusion and the patient's preferences.
Single oral dose: 30 mg.
Can be used up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse.
Generally more effective than levonorgestrel during days 3–5.
Delays ovulation; it is not effective once ovulation has already occurred.
Progestogen-containing contraception must generally be delayed for 5 days after taking UPA.
Single oral dose: 1.5 mg.
Take as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours.
Effectiveness decreases as time passes; some guidelines permit use up to 120 hours, but it is less reliable later.
Ongoing hormonal contraception can generally be started or resumed immediately.
Availability, licensing and local protocols may differ. Always check the applicable national or institutional guideline.

rows: Within 5 days, subject to ovulation-based guidance
Ideally within 72 hours; effectiveness declines later
Less effective than UPA, particularly later

blocks.text: Important counselling point: oral emergency contraception mainly works by delaying or preventing ovulation. It does not terminate an established pregnancy and does not protect against unprotected intercourse later in the same cycle.
Establish the time since intercourse. Record the exact date and approximate time of each episode, including any earlier episodes in the cycle.
Discuss the copper IUD. Offer it as the most effective option when suitable and acceptable to the patient, particularly if oral EC may be less reliable.
Select an oral option if preferred or appropriate. Consider elapsed time, likely ovulation, medicines, body weight and recent progestogen use.

Explain what happens next. Discuss when ongoing contraception can begin, the need for condoms or abstinence during the method's initiation period, and the fact that EC does not cover later intercourse.
Arrange follow-up. Advise pregnancy testing and discuss STI assessment, menstrual changes and when to seek medical attention.

content_groups.group_title: Choosing between UPA and LNG: important interactions

blocks.text: After UPA: wait 5 full days before starting or restarting progestogen-containing contraception, because progestogen may reduce UPA's ability to delay ovulation. Use condoms or abstain during the waiting period and then for the recommended backup period after restarting the chosen method.
After LNG: hormonal contraception can generally be started or resumed immediately, with method-appropriate backup.
Enzyme-inducing medication: the copper IUD is generally preferred because enzyme induction can reduce oral EC effectiveness. Seek local specialist guidance if an IUD is unsuitable.
Higher body weight/BMI: oral EC effectiveness may be reduced, especially with LNG. Do not deny oral EC; discuss the copper IUD or UPA where appropriate and follow local guidance.
Dose: 1.5 mg orally once.
Take as soon as possible.
If vomiting occurs within approximately 3 hours, another dose is generally needed; confirm the product-specific guidance.
It can cause nausea, headache, abdominal discomfort, breast tenderness or temporary menstrual changes.
Dose: 30 mg orally once.
Take within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse.
If vomiting occurs within approximately 3 hours, a repeat dose is generally required.
Explain the 5-day delay before starting or restarting progestogen-containing contraception.
Before insertion:
Assess whether pregnancy can reasonably be excluded.
Review medical and sexual-health history.
Assess for relevant contraindications and possible pelvic infection.
Explain insertion, likely discomfort, bleeding changes and risks.
Obtain informed consent and arrange insertion by a trained clinician.
If there is a significant risk of an STI, follow local guidance for testing and management. The assessment should not unnecessarily delay time-sensitive care.
Advise the patient to:
Take a pregnancy test about 3 weeks after the most recent unprotected intercourse, even if emergency contraception was used.
Test sooner if the period is significantly delayed, particularly more than 7 days beyond the expected date, or is unusually light.
Seek urgent assessment for severe or persistent lower abdominal pain, fainting, heavy bleeding or other concerning symptoms, particularly if pregnancy is possible.
Arrange STI testing when indicated.
Seek advice if vomiting occurs soon after taking oral EC.
Use condoms or another effective method for subsequent intercourse, according to the timing requirements of the chosen ongoing contraceptive.

Do not delay time-sensitive oral EC merely because a pregnancy test cannot yet detect a very recent conception. However, an IUD should only be inserted when pregnancy can reasonably be excluded according to the applicable protocol.

items: Scenario A: Condom broke 24 hours ago

blocks.text: A patient presents the day after a condom failure and wants to avoid pregnancy.
Approach: establish timing and other intercourse, discuss the copper IUD, and offer an appropriate oral option if preferred. Explain follow-up testing and ongoing contraception.
Key point: both LNG and UPA are options within this timeframe; choice depends on patient preference, suitability and interactions.

items: Scenario B: Unprotected intercourse 4 days ago

blocks.text: Approach: discuss the copper IUD as the most effective option and UPA 30 mg as the preferred oral option in many circumstances. LNG may be less effective this late.
Key point: do not automatically assume that all oral EC methods are equally effective throughout the 5-day period.

items: Scenario C: Patient taking an enzyme-inducing medicine

blocks.text: Approach: review the exact medication and duration of use, explain the interaction, and prioritise assessment for a copper IUD if suitable. Follow local specialist guidance if insertion is not possible.
Key point: do not prescribe oral EC without considering drug interactions.
Scenario D: Patient has already taken UPA and wants to restart her pill
Approach: explain that she should generally wait 5 days before restarting progestogen-containing contraception, then use condoms or abstain for the recommended backup period after restarting.
Key point: this differs from LNG, after which hormonal contraception can generally be resumed immediately.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most effective emergency contraceptive?
The copper IUD. It also provides ongoing contraception.
Q2. What is the dose of ulipristal acetate?
30 mg orally as a single dose, within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse.
Q3. What is the dose of levonorgestrel?
1.5 mg orally as a single dose, taken as soon as possible. It is most effective when taken early.
Q4. Does emergency contraception cause an abortion?
No. Emergency contraceptive pills primarily delay or prevent ovulation. They do not terminate an established pregnancy.
Q5. Can a patient become pregnant after taking emergency contraception?
Yes. No oral method is completely effective, and emergency contraception does not protect against subsequent unprotected intercourse.
Q6. When should the patient perform a pregnancy test?
Approximately 3 weeks after the most recent unprotected intercourse, or sooner if her period is significantly delayed or symptoms raise concern.
Q7. Why must progestogen contraception be delayed after UPA?
Progestogen may interfere with UPA's effect on ovulation. The patient should generally wait 5 days before starting or restarting progestogen-containing contraception.
Q8. What if the patient vomits after taking an emergency contraceptive pill?
If vomiting occurs within approximately 3 hours, a repeat dose is generally recommended. Confirm the product-specific instructions.
Q9. Does emergency contraception protect against STIs?
No. Assess the need for STI testing, treatment and condoms.
Q10. What is the role of emergency contraception following sexual assault?

Provide compassionate, non-judgemental care; assess immediate safety; offer emergency contraception, STI assessment and prophylaxis where indicated; consider HIV post-exposure prophylaxis within the recommended window; and offer appropriate forensic, psychological and safeguarding support according to the patient's wishes and local protocol.
Failing to establish the exact timing of intercourse.
Forgetting to ask about earlier unprotected intercourse.
Presenting LNG and UPA as equally effective late in the 5-day window.
Forgetting the 5-day delay before restarting progestogen contraception after UPA.
Claiming that emergency contraception protects against STIs or later intercourse.
Failing to arrange a pregnancy test.
Ignoring drug interactions, patient preferences or the copper IUD option.
Being judgemental or failing to consider sexual assault.
